A1-A2.headline: The Mighty Battleships of the Sea

pages.text: Battleships were very big, strong ships. They had large guns and thick metal armor. For many years, they were the most powerful ships in the world. They started in the late 1880s. They stayed important until aircraft carriers took over in the 1940s.
pages.caption: USS Iowa firing a large broadside.

evidence.fileTitle: File:BB61 USS Iowa BB61 broadside USN.jpg

pages.text: In the late 1880s, Britain built the Royal Sovereign ships. People call these the first pre-dreadnought battleships. They were very strong and could travel far on the ocean. They had four big guns and many smaller guns for protection. Many countries built ships like these.
pages.caption: The German Brandenburg had six heavy guns.

evidence.articleCaption: The German Brandenburg, which carried six heavy guns, rather than the standard four

pages.text: In 1905, Britain launched the HMS Dreadnought. This ship was very different. It did not use medium guns. Instead, it had ten big guns. This change made all other ships look old. Soon, every country wanted to build their own big-gun ships.
pages.caption: HMS Dreadnought was a new design.

pages.text: Later, countries agreed to stop building so many ships. The Washington Naval Treaty set limits. In World War II, planes became more important than big ships. Battleships were still used, but they were not the main force anymore. They were often used for secondary jobs.

Some people thought battleships were too expensive. They wanted smaller, cheaper boats. Even so, the big ships stayed for a long time. Today, many old battleships are museums. They are still symbols of a country's power and history on the sea.
pages.caption: USS Iowa sailing in the 1980s.

evidence.articleCaption: USN carrier group led by USS Iowa in 1987
evidence.articleSection: Cold War: end of the battleship era

B1-B2.headline: The Rise and Fall of the Great Battleships

pages.text: Battleships were massive, heavily armored warships that served as the backbone of naval fleets from the late 1880s. Designed to dominate the seas with their large-caliber guns, these vessels were the most formidable warships of their time. Their reign lasted until the 1940s, when aircraft carriers emerged as the new masters of naval warfare.
pages.caption: USS Iowa firing a full broadside.

evidence.fileTitle: File:BB61 USS Iowa BB61 broadside USN.jpg

pages.text: The modern battleship era began in the late 1880s with the British Royal Sovereign class. These ships were the first to be called pre-dreadnoughts. They featured high sides for ocean travel, thick armor, and a standard layout of four large guns. This design became the blueprint for naval powers globally as they expanded their fleets.
pages.caption: The German Brandenburg carried six heavy guns.

evidence.articleCaption: The German Brandenburg, which carried six heavy guns, rather than the standard four

pages.text: Following the Russo-Japanese War, the launch of HMS Dreadnought changed everything. By replacing medium guns with a uniform battery of ten large guns, it made all existing ships obsolete. This innovation sparked a global naval arms race, as every major power scrambled to build their own all-big-gun ships to maintain their maritime strength.
pages.caption: HMS Dreadnought changed naval design forever.

pages.text: Following World War I, nations signed treaties like the Washington Naval Treaty to limit battleship construction and prevent costly arms races. During World War II, the rise of air power shifted the focus away from battleships. While they still participated in significant battles, they were often relegated to secondary roles as carriers took the lead.

Even as their dominance faded, battleships remained powerful symbols of national pride. Some strategists had questioned their value as early as the 1880s, favoring smaller, cheaper vessels. Today, many of these historic ships serve as museum ships, preserving the legacy of an era when these iron giants ruled the world's oceans.
pages.caption: USS Iowa underway in 1987.

C1-C2.headline: The Evolution and Strategic Decline of the Capital Ship

pages.text: As the quintessential capital ships of the late 19th century, battleships represented the pinnacle of naval engineering. These heavily armored, large-caliber gun platforms dominated maritime strategy from the 1880s until the mid-20th century. Their eventual obsolescence was precipitated by the ascendancy of the aircraft carrier, which fundamentally altered the nature of naval engagement during the 1940s.
pages.caption: USS Iowa firing a full broadside.

evidence.fileTitle: File:BB61 USS Iowa BB61 broadside USN.jpg

pages.text: The genesis of the modern battleship can be traced to the British Royal Sovereign class, which established the pre-dreadnought paradigm. These vessels integrated high freeboards for blue-water capability with robust armor and standardized heavy armament. This architecture served as the definitive template for global naval expansion, setting the standard for subsequent battleship development across major maritime powers.
pages.caption: The German Brandenburg carried six heavy guns.

evidence.articleCaption: The German Brandenburg, which carried six heavy guns, rather than the standard four

pages.text: Following the 1904–1905 conflict, the commissioning of HMS Dreadnought marked a radical departure from existing naval doctrine. By adopting an all-big-gun armament, the vessel rendered the previous generation of ships effectively redundant. This technological leap precipitated an intense international naval arms race, as powers sought to modernize their fleets to match the new standard of maritime superiority.
pages.caption: HMS Dreadnought changed naval design forever.

pages.text: Interwar diplomatic efforts, notably the Washington Naval Treaty, sought to curtail the escalating naval arms race through strict construction limitations. By World War II, the strategic utility of the battleship had waned as air power became the decisive factor in naval combat. Despite their continued participation in major engagements, their role was increasingly secondary to the power projection of carriers.

Despite early skepticism from the Jeune École, the battleship remained the arbiter of naval combat for decades. These vessels functioned as potent symbols of state power, retaining significant diplomatic and psychological weight long after their tactical utility had diminished. Today, preserved as museum ships, they stand as enduring monuments to a bygone era of naval supremacy, though their historical impact remains a subject of ongoing debate.
